newsitem.title: USA: Lott says he unafraid of Clinton disaster aid veto.
newsitem.headline: Lott says he unafraid of Clinton disaster aid veto.

text.p: The Senate's top Republican said Tuesday he was not scared by President Clinton's vow to veto a $8.4 billion emergency spending bill, calling it a "hollow, empty threat."

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott called on White House officials to sit down with Republicans to work out a compromise allowing Clinton to sign the measure, aiding more than 30 states hit by floods and bad weather.

Republicans attached an unrelated provision to the bill to automatically keep the government running next year if Congress and the White House could not agree on spending bills. Clinton adamantly opposed that plan.
"If all they're going to do is stomp their feet and threaten vetoes, go right ahead," Lott said.

"I would suggest in the alternative that we act like big boys, and talk it through, and work it out ... But if they think they're going to bluff us into taking this out at this point, it won't work," he told reporters.
Republican leaders were eager to avoid a repeat of two unpopular government shutdowns during fiscal 1996, which voters blamed on their party.
Clinton said the automatic spending plan would provide $18 billion less for domestic spending than Republicans agreed to as part of a new balanced budget deal.
It would fund government programmes at 100 percent of the previous year's level if spending bills were not approved.

"While the goal of ensuring that the government does not shut down again ... is a worthy one, such a provision is clearly extraneous to this emergency disaster relief legisaltion," the White House said in a letter to Congress.
The letter renewed Clinton's veto threat.

House and Senate lawmakers Tuesday began negotiations to work out a final version of the bill. The bill included $5.5 billion to help weather-ravaged states. It also included nearly $2 billion to fund American peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and U.S. military flights in the Gulf.

The automatic spending provision was the most contentious issue, but there were other ticklish questions to be resolved including a Senate provision making it easier to build roads on federal lands in Alaska and sampling for the 2000 census.
Lott said he was open to a compromise on spending. Congressional leaders begin a Memorial Day recess on Friday.
